title: 3-Week IB Global Politics Revision Plan
summary: IB Global Politics revision plan for November: triage topics, strengthen case studies, practise timed papers and protect rest across three weeks.
body_markdown:
Three weeks before an IB examination session can feel strangely short. There is too much content to revisit, yet enough time to make poor priorities expensive.


A useful **IB Global Politics revision plan** does not attempt to relearn the entire course. It identifies weak areas, strengthens a versatile bank of evidence, and gradually shifts from open-book practice to timed performance. If you are sitting several November examinations, it must also leave room for your other subjects and for sleep.


One important detail applies to November 2026 candidates: the revised Global Politics course was first assessed in May 2026. Under this model, Paper 1 is a source-based paper shared by SL and HL, Paper 2 tests thematic studies through extended responses, and Paper 3 is an additional stimulus-based paper for HL. Confirm your exact schedule and requirements with your coordinator before planning.


### Your three-week overview


Week Main priority Practical outcome


Week 1 Diagnose and organise A ranked topic list and usable evidence bank


Week 2 Apply and improve Better source analysis, arguments and timed writing


Week 3 Rehearse and recover Exam-ready routines without last-minute exhaustion


Keep the plan flexible. A student sitting two November subjects may have more Global Politics time than someone sitting five. Instead of copying fixed daily hours, assign a realistic share of your available revision blocks to each subject.


### Week 1: Triage your Global Politics knowledge


The first week should answer a simple question: *Where will another hour of work help most?*


Begin with a diagnostic task under limited time. Choose representative questions for the papers you will sit and attempt plans or responses without notes. The point is not to generate a reassuring score. It is to expose friction.


Sort each syllabus area into three categories:


- **Secure:** you can explain concepts, select relevant examples and build an argument.
- **Unstable:** you recognise the material but struggle to apply or evaluate it.
- **Priority:** you cannot yet produce a defensible answer under time pressure.


Spend most of the week on unstable and priority areas. Revisiting familiar notes feels productive because recognition comes easily, but recognition is not the same as retrieval.


### Build a flexible evidence bank


Global Politics rewards evidence when it is relevant and analysed. Create a compact case-study bank around the core theme and thematic studies required by your course. For every example, record:


- the political issue and context
- the actors and their interests
- two or three useful concepts
- competing perspectives
- the claim the evidence could support
- a limitation or counterargument


Avoid memorising one example for one predicted question. A smaller collection of adaptable examples is more useful than a long catalogue of facts you cannot connect to an argument.


RevisionDojo’s Study Notes and Flashcards can help you compress definitions and evidence, while AI Chat can test whether you genuinely understand a concept. Use AI explanations as prompts for checking your thinking, not as substitutes for your course materials or teacher guidance.


A workable Week 1 pattern is four focused Global Politics sessions: one diagnostic, two topic-repair sessions and one evidence-retrieval session. Keep at least one evening light if other examinations demand attention.


### Week 2: Turn knowledge into answers


Week 2 is where **IB Global Politics revision** becomes performance practice. Knowledge matters, but marks depend on what you do with it under the demands of each paper.


For Paper 1, practise identifying a source’s claim, perspective, purpose and limitations before writing. Compare sources precisely rather than describing them one after another. Then connect source material to relevant political concepts and contextual knowledge where the question requires it.


For Paper 2, alternate between essay plans and complete responses. A useful plan should contain:


- a direct answer to the question
- clearly separated lines of argument
- relevant political concepts
- specific evidence
- counterclaims or alternative perspectives
- an evaluative conclusion


HL students should also schedule focused Paper 3 practice. Work from unfamiliar stimuli, retrieve appropriate case-study evidence and practise constructing an argument rather than unloading everything you know about a global political challenge.


RevisionDojo’s[guide to building an IB Global Politics study group](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-global-politics-study-group-fall) offers a useful model for discussing arguments and testing interpretations with classmates. Keep group sessions structured: agree on one question, compare plans, challenge evidence and finish with an individual rewrite.


### Use marked attempts as data


Every practice response should produce one action. It might be “answer the command term earlier,” “compare sources directly,” or “explain why this evidence changes the argument.” A page of broad feedback is less useful than one correction deliberately applied to the next task.


Use RevisionDojo’s Questionbank for targeted practice, then check your reasoning with the Grading tools. The Coursework Library can help you recognise disciplined analysis, although examination answers have different constraints and should not imitate coursework structure blindly. If a recurring weakness remains difficult to diagnose, a teacher or RevisionDojo Tutor can offer targeted guidance.


A student says they scheduled flexibility while a cat occupies the calendar and claims it scheduled the time first.


### Week 3: Rehearse the examination, then reduce the load


The final week should not be the heaviest. It should be the most specific.


Early in the week, sit timed papers in RevisionDojo’s Exam mode. Use official timing and permitted materials, remove notifications, and do not pause to consult notes. Predicted Papers and Mock Exams can provide additional rehearsal, but no practice resource can guarantee what will appear in November.


After each attempt, separate problems into three groups:


Problem Best response


Missing knowledge Repair one narrow content gap


Weak reasoning Rewrite the argument or paragraph


Poor timing Practise a shorter timed section


Do not immediately sit another full paper to erase a disappointing result. Review first. Otherwise, you risk rehearsing the same mistake at greater speed.


In the middle of Week 3, run short retrieval sessions. Recite concepts without notes, match examples to possible arguments, and build rapid outlines from unfamiliar prompts. This preserves recall without adding the fatigue of repeated full papers.


During the final 24-48 hours, lower the volume. Review a short evidence sheet, check practical arrangements and stop at a planned time. Sleep supports attention and recall; late-night cramming often sacrifices both precisely when you need them.


### A flexible daily structure for several subjects


A revision plan should survive ordinary disruption. Use blocks rather than a minute-by-minute timetable:


- **Block A:** the nearest or weakest subject
- **Block B:** Global Politics retrieval or targeted practice
- **Block C:** another subject or a marked Global Politics response
- **Short close:** review errors and decide tomorrow’s first task


On demanding school days, one focused Global Politics block may be enough. On freer days, complete two blocks with a substantial break between them. Protect one lighter period each week and avoid treating rest as time that must later be repaid.


### What to do when the plan slips


A missed session is not a reason to compress two days into one. Remove the least valuable task and continue.


Preserve the essentials: diagnostic triage, active retrieval, paper-specific practice, feedback and at least one realistic timed rehearsal. Cut decorative tasks first, including rewriting attractive notes or building elaborate timetables.


The calm advantage in revision comes from knowing what not to do. Three weeks cannot make preparation perfect, but they can make it deliberate. Start by finding the gaps, convert knowledge into arguments, and finish by rehearsing the conditions in which that knowledge must work.


RevisionDojo brings that sequence together. Practise weak areas in the **Questionbank** , use Study Notes and Flashcards for retrieval, seek feedback through AI Chat and Grading tools, then sit timed papers in **Exam mode** . The goal is not to feel endlessly busy. It is to arrive in November familiar with the decisions the examination will ask you to make.
